title: Pyramid Texts of Unas: Utterances 277-301 (antechamber, east wall)
source: Pyramid of Unas, Saqqara, antechamber, east wall (photograph: L. F. Husson for A. Piankoff 1968, via Pyramid Texts Online) + TLA transliteration (ed. D. Topmann, CC BY-SA 4.0) + English of S. A. B. Mercer (1952, public domain in the US)
description: The Pyramid Texts on the east wall of the antechamber in the pyramid of Unas (c. 2350 BCE), utterance by utterance, with the TLA transliteration and Mercer's English.
introduction:
The Pyramid Texts are the oldest large body of Egyptian religious writing: spells, called utterances, for the resurrection of the dead king, his protection, his meals and his ascent to the sky, cut in vertical columns of hieroglyphs on the walls of the burial apartments of late Old Kingdom pyramids. The pyramid of Unas at Saqqara, the last king of the 5th Dynasty (about 2375-2345 BCE), is the first to carry them. Its sarcophagus chamber, the passage to the antechamber, the antechamber and the corridor hold 649 numbered columns of text; this library gives every column, wall by wall, in seventeen entries (227 different utterances, some of them inscribed more than once).

This entry is the east wall of the antechamber: 36 columns of hieroglyphs, Sethe's W 532-566, which follow each other from the right-hand (south) edge of the photograph. It holds the utterances 278, 277, 279, 281, 280, 282, 283, 284, 285, 286, 287, 288, 290, 289, 291, 292, 293, 294, 295, 296-297, 298, 299, 300, 301. The TLA numbers one extra column in PT 293 as 544+1.

Each section is one utterance. The Egyptian is the transliteration of the Thesaurus Linguae Aegyptiae (edition by Doris Topmann), with Sethe's Unas column number (W) before each column; a number ending in 'a' marks the offering label at the foot of a column. Signs restored by the editor are in square brackets, signs the scribe left out in angle brackets, damaged signs in half brackets. The English is Samuel A. B. Mercer's translation of 1952. Mercer translates Sethe's composite text made from all the pyramids that have an utterance, so his wording can include clauses that are not in the Unas copy, and his section numbers (134a, 134b ...) are Sethe's paragraph numbers, not column numbers; he writes 'N.' where the wall has the king's name. The photograph shows the whole wall; each section's note gives its columns counted from the edge where the text on that wall begins.
translator_notes: Mercer's separate headings, postscripts and variants taken from other pyramids are left out.
Letters follow the sacred-texts transcription of Mercer: ȝ stands for aleph and ‘ for ayin; letters underlined in the printed book are given as ḏ, ṯ, ẖ.
Sethe's section numbers are kept as printed in that transcription, including a few misprints (for example '146.' for 141b in Utterance 215).
The TLA has no hieroglyphic encoding for these texts, so only the transliteration is shown.

439bN. is Geb. Hmṯ-serpent, brother of hmṯ.t-serpent,
439cshould thy father, the ḏ‘‘miw, die?
Utterance 297.
440aThe hand of N. which is come upon thee--
440bit is a violent one which is come upon thee,
440cit is the mȝfd.t-lynx, which is in the house of life.
440dShe strikes thee in thy face; she scratches thee in thine eyes,
441aso that thou fallest in thy dung and glidest in thy urine.
441bFall, lie down, glide away, so that thy mother Nut may see thee.

442aTo say: Rē‘ dawns, his uraeus on his head,
442bagainst this serpent, which is come out of the earth, (and) which is under the fingers of N.
442cHe (N.) cuts off thy head with this knife, which was in the hand of the mȝfd.t-lynx, [which lives in the house of life];
443ahe draws, (the teeth) which are upon (in) thy mouth; he saps thy poison
443bwith those four strings, which were in the service of the sandals of Osiris.
443cSerpent (beast), lie down; bull, glide away.

444aTo say: The uraeus-serpent is for heaven; the centipede of Horus is for the earth.
444bHorus had a sandal as he advanced (towards) the master of the house, the bull of the hole,
444cthe combat-serpent. N. will not be beaten,
444d(for) his protective sycamore is the protective sycamore of N., his refuge is the refuge of N.
444eWhom N. finds in his way, him he eats for himself bit by bit.

445aTo say: O H̱rti of Nsȝ.t, ferryman of the ’Iḳh.t-boat, made by Khnum,
445bbring this (boat) to N. N. is Seker of R-Śṯȝ.w.
445cN. is on the way to the place of Seker, chief of Pḏw-š.
445dIt is our brother who is bringing this (boat) for these bridge-girderers (?) of the desert.

translation.text:
446aTo say: Thy established-offering is thine, O Niw (Nun) together with Nn.t (Naunet),
446bye two sources of the gods, protecting the gods with their (your) shade.
446cThy established-offering is thine, O Amūn together with Amūnet,
446dye two sources of the gods, protecting the gods with their (your) shade.
447aThy established-offering is thine, O Atum together with the two lions, ye double power of the gods, yourselves, who created yourselves,
447bthat is, Shu together with Tefnut, (who) created the gods, begat the gods, established the gods.
448aSay ye to your father (Ptaḥ)
448bthat N. has given to you your established-offering, that N. has satisfied you with your due.
448cYe shall (or, should) not hinder N. when he ferries to the horizon to him.
449aN. knows him, knows his name. Nḥi is, his name, Nḥi lord of the year is his name;
449bhe with the warrior's arm, Horus who is over the śẖd.w of heaven, who causes Rē‘ to live every day.
450aHe will rebuild N.; he will cause N. to live every day.
450bN. comes to thee, Horus of H̱ȝ.t; N. comes to thee, Horus of Šsm.t;
450cN. comes to thee, Horus of the East.
451aBehold, N. brings to thee thy great left eye as healer.
451bTake it, the intact (one), to thyself from N.; its water is in it, being intact;
451cits blood is in it, being intact; its breath is in it, being intact.
452aEnter into it; take possession of it, in this thy name of "Sacred Ḥḳ3ś" (a god),
452bthat thou mayest approach to it in this thy name of "Rē‘"'.
453aPut it on thy brow, in this, its name of "choice oil",
453bthat thou mayest rejoice in it, in this its name of "willow-tree",
454athat thou mayest sparkle thereby among the gods, in this its name of "that which sparkles", (or, "ṯḥnw.t-oil"),
454bthat thou mayest be pleased with it in this its name of "oil of pleasure", (or, "ḥkn.w-oil").
454c(Then) will the Rnn-wt.t-serpent love thee.
455aStand there, great reed-float, like Wp-wȝ.wt,
455bfilled with thy splendour, come forth from the horizon,
455cafter thou hast taken possession of the white crown in the water-springs, great and mighty, which are in the south of Libya,
456a(like) Sebek, lord of Bȝẖ.w.
456bThou journeyest to thy fields, thou passest through thy kśb.t-woods,
456cthy nose breathes the fragrance of the Šsmt.t-land.
456dThou causest the ka of N. to approach his side,
456elike as thy Wig (deified) approaches thee.
457aPurify N., make N. bright
457bin this thy jackal-lake, O jackal, where thou purifiest the gods.
457cThou art become a soul, thou art become pre-eminent (sharp), (like.) Horus lord of the green-stone--(to say) four times--(like) the two green falcons.
